vignette:
He is a 49-year-old married architect who first begins to unravel after witnessing a devastating collapse at a construction site several years ago. He had been there for a routine meeting, reviewing a final set of plans with the contractor and walking the perimeter of the building with a hard hat tucked under his arm. He remembers the day in sharp fragments: the metallic sound of work overhead, the vibration in the ground, the sudden shout that cuts through the usual noise. Then the scaffolding gives way. In an instant, what had felt like a normal worksite becomes chaos—dust, steel, screaming, men running in different directions. He does not physically lose anyone that day, but he sees a laborer pinned beneath debris, another bleeding from the head, and the look on one worker’s face as he realizes someone is trapped. That image stays with him more than anything.

In the days after, he tells himself he is fortunate. He returns to work quickly, because that is what he has always done. He has built his life around precision, control, and problem-solving, and he initially tries to manage the memory the same way he manages a project: by organizing it, compartmentalizing it, pushing it into a box he believes he can keep closed. But the sight of scaffolding begins to tighten his chest. When he drives past construction sites, his eyes go immediately to the upper floors, the harnesses, the edges where something might fail. He starts taking different routes to avoid passing the site where it happened. He says he is just saving time, but he knows he is also avoiding the surge of nausea that hits him when he gets close.

At work, his concentration becomes less reliable. As an architect, he depends on attention to detail, yet now he finds himself rereading the same drawing several times, unable to trust that he has absorbed it. He becomes increasingly irritable with contractors and colleagues, especially when they minimize safety concerns or rush through inspections. He hears his own voice sounding sharper than he intends. At home, his wife notices that he is quieter, more distant, and easier to startle. A dropped dish or a sudden bang in the house can send his body into an immediate jolt, as if he is back on the site. He does not like to admit that he sleeps poorly. He lies awake replaying the collapse in his mind, not in a coherent way, but in flashes that arrive without permission—dust in the air, the crack of metal, the worker’s voice yelling for help. Some nights he finally dozes off only to wake abruptly, heart pounding, with no clear dream he can explain.

Over time, his world narrows. He stops volunteering for site visits unless absolutely necessary. He is careful not to let his children see how uneasy he feels around unfinished structures, because he does not want them to think their father is afraid of his own profession. But the truth is that the job, which once gave him pride, now carries a constant undercurrent of dread. He starts imagining worst-case scenarios while reviewing plans: a beam failing, a handrail giving way, someone hurt because he missed something small. He has always been conscientious, but now responsibility feels heavier, almost dangerous. He becomes preoccupied with what he could have done differently that day, even though he knows, rationally, that he did not cause the collapse. The guilt lingers anyway, joined by anger at the unpredictability of it all and shame that he cannot simply move on.

He notices that he is not the same with his wife. She says he is “there, but not there.” He hears it as an accusation, though she means it with concern. He wants to explain that part of him is still on that site, still hearing the screams, still bracing for the moment when something falls again. But he struggles to put this into words. Instead, he withdraws. He spends more time alone in his study, staring at unfinished sketches or quietly making revisions to plans that do not need revising. Even when he is home, his mind tends to scan for danger. He checks locks, windows, and alarms with a habit that has become more ritual than reason.

By the time he comes in for help, he describes himself as functional on the outside and “always on alert” underneath. He is exhausted by the effort of keeping his composure. He wants to be the capable man his family and colleagues expect, but he is increasingly aware that the event has altered his sense of safety in the world. The collapse is over, yet it continues to live in his body, in his sleep, in the way he watches every structure with a measure of suspicion, as if the ground itself can no longer be trusted.
